newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik leader seeks end to clashes, troops' support.
newsitem.headline: Tajik leader seeks end to clashes, troops' support.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov has demanded an end to clashes between rival armed groups in the former Soviet republic and appealed to government troops to remain loyal.
Fighting died down in the capital Dushanbe on Sunday, the second day of violence, but Russian news agencies said clashes continued to the south of the city.
Tajikistan has just emerged from a four-year civil war in which the government faced opposition Islamist guerrillas, but the weekend clashes involved rival warlords who are nominally pro-government.

"The people who provoke these military clashes are connected with the economic mafia, the drugs mafia and the criminal world," an official statement quoted Rakhmonov as saying during a meeting of Tajikistan's Security Council.
It said he had issued a call to servicemen to "abide by their oath of allegiance, not give in to the influence of criminal groups and refrain from criminal actions".
An aide to Rakhmonov said the president had told the rival groups to stop fighting within three days or face destruction.
Rakhmonov signed a peace deal in June which was intended to end the civil war which erupted after the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.

But the peace is fragile in Tajikistan, a mountainous country of 5.7 million people which has been carved up into independent fiefdoms controlled by maverick armed groups similar to those in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Fighting between rival armed bands flared in Dushanbe on Saturday over the killing of an uncle of Sukhrob Kasimov, an Interior Ministry commander.
Kasimov's forces seized control of a northern district in the capital from Yakub Salimov, a customs chief and former interior minister.

Russian news agencies said fighting in the Fakhrobad Valley about 30 km (20 miles) south of Dushanbe involved another powerful government commander, Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, who has mutinied twice in the past.
He has threatened to try to oust Kasimov from Dushanbe.
Rakhmonov's ability to resist Kudoyberdyev is unclear but he might seek help from a Commonwealth of Independent States peacekeeping force dominated by Russia.
Russia, which is worried by violence on what it regards as its soft "under-belly", has about 20,000 troops in Tajikistan carrying out peacekeeping duties and guarding borders.
